en: Abhidhānottara 11 = palm-leaf manuscript = Raghu Vīra’s manuscript reproduction by Lokesh Chandra
Now I shall further explain the successive divisions of the families,
along with the arrangement of the seats (pīṭha) and so forth according to their sequence, as well as the division of the directions and their order.
Through this supreme great yoga, the sovereignty of yoga is accomplished.
The mandala arisen from the vajra-body is the supreme of all mandalas.
Then all the Blessed Tathāgatas, having again gathered in assembly with the Vīra-yoginīs, bowed down to Mahāvajradhara, the Lord of Great Bliss, their eyes blossoming with intense joy.
With the procedures of the sequences of lowering and raising,
and with the thrusts of the tips of their hands from the left and right, they performed the water-offering.
With slight smiles, side-long glances, the graceful movement of released eyebrows,
and the joyous blossoming of the eyes— O Mother, bend this world with these gestures!
Exhorting Śauri with this song,
all the yoginīs remained stationed within the great maṇḍala of supreme bliss.
"O Blessed One, please speak the reality of the supremely auspicious maṇḍala,
which begins with the Great Bliss-Vajra of Great Passion and is the great bliss of all Buddhas."
We have obtained the supreme great bliss, Alalala! O Great Bliss, the island of all the Tathāgatas!
By this song being sung, they are utterly liberated from existence.
For the Tathāgatas, who are utterly pure, indeed conceive of the maṇḍala.

Then the Blessed One, Mahāsukha-Vajrasattva, with a smiling face blossomed like a lotus, his eyes like full-blown lotuses, and his gaze fixed on the tips of his playfully arched eyebrows, uttered this reality within the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind— flashes as flickering as waves of lightning:
"That which is called a mandala, a mandala, resides in the heart of vajra-gnosis."
Through the application of mere conceptualization, the mandala is the supreme vajra.
Resembling the full moon of the mandala, free from great passion,
garlanded with white rays, it is wondrous like another bodhicitta.
The entire universe consists of blue flames, impelled by wind and fire;
it is the divine mandala of the Vajra-sun, composed of the half-moon.
The eight-petaled mandala, blazing and resembling the sun among suns,
is the mandala of the Vajra-jewel, the means for achieving the birth of the Surata.
It has eight petals in full bloom, crowded with the region of the pericarp;
in the lotus, it is shaped like a lotus, that mandala born of divine passion.
The delightful triangular maṇḍala, resembling a network of lotuses at the heart,
which performs the rites of true devotion, is the maṇḍala of the Vajrī for the accomplishment of rites.
Such are the arrangements of the mandalas, beginning with these and ending with Nṛtyāgra;
they were fashioned exactly as they are by Vajrasattva, the Protector.
Samantabhadra, the self of all, having undergone transformation into the space-element,
should manifest a peaked pavilion within the delightful abode of the space-element.
Within the interior of the gabled chamber, one should arrange the five mandalas;
one should place them in their respective positions upon a beautiful universal lotus seat.
In the center of the middle mandala, one should visualize Heruka,
possessing the colors and forms previously described, comfortably seated with Vārāhī.
In Pullīramalaya to the east is Pracaṇḍā, the consort of Khaṇḍakapālin; in Jālandhara to the north is Caṇḍākṣī, the consort of Mahākaṅkāla;
and in Oḍiyāna to the west is PrabHāvatī, the consort of Kaṅkāla.
In the south, at Arbuda, is Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrin with a large nose;
thus is the middle maṇḍala.
In the center of this very eastern maṇḍala, in Godāvarī, are Surāvairiṇī and Vīramatī;
in the east, at Rāmeśvara, are Amitābha and Kharvarī.
In the north, at Devikoṭa, she is Vajraprabhā Laṅkeśvarī;
in the west, in Mālava, she is Vajradeha Drumacchāyā;
in the south, in Kāmarūpa, she is Aṅkurikā Airāvatī.
In the center of the northern mandala, at Odra, are Vajrajaṭila and Mahābhairavā; in the east, at Triśakuni, are Mahāvīra and Vāyuvegā;
in the north, at Kośalā, are Vajrahūṃkāra and Surābhakṣī.
In Kaliṅga in the west is Subhadra and Śyāmādevī;
in Lampāka in the south is Vajrabhadra and Subhadrā;
in the center of the western maṇḍala, in Kāñcika, are Mahābhairava and Hayakarṇā.
In the east, at Himālaya, is Virūpākṣī and Khagānanā; in the north, at Pretapurī, are Mahābalā and Cakravegā;
in the west, at Gṛhadevatā, are Ratnavajrā and Khaṇḍarohā.
In the south, in Saurāṣṭra, are Hayagrīva and Śauṇḍinī.
In the center of the southern mandala, on Suvarṇadvīpa, is Ākāśagarbha and Cakravarminī; in the eastern city is Heruka and Suvīrā;
in the north, in Sindhu, is Padmanarteśvara and Mahābalā.
In the western Maru is Vairocanacakravartinī;
in Kulatā in the south is Vajrasattvamahāvīryā.
The heroes, Khaṇḍakapāla and the others, together with Pracaṇḍā and the rest, are all deformed, faceless, six-armed, and three-eyed; they stand in the *ālīḍha* posture.

Delighted by their *mudrās*, the goddesses are naked with disheveled hair, embracing [their consorts] while holding a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, a *ḍamaru*, a flaying knife, and a vajra-bell. They are firmly encircled by the two knees of the goddesses, engaged in great sexual union, and overwhelmed by the savor of the bliss of that great passion.

In the center, at the position of the lord of the maṇḍala, in the four corners upon the vases are skull-cups filled with the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). One should truly place [these] in the corners of the other four maṇḍalas; outside the vases and skull-cups, in the corner regions, are the four goddesses beginning with Ḍākinī.
Ardhanārīśvarī has three faces and three eyes, stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, is naked, has loose hair, and is empowered by the five mudrās.
The fivefold maṇḍala is encircled by a vajra-fence; one should draw a variegated circle of flames on the exterior.
She is praised by all the heroes and yoginīs while mounted upon a corpse atop a universal lotus.

To the east, in the four gates of the body and so forth, is Kākāsyā, with a hollow and fierce countenance, holding a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, a bell, and a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*); she has three eyes, three faces, loose hair, is naked, multicolored, stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, rests upon a corpse on a universal lotus, dwells in the midst of a circle of flames, and is adorned with the five mudrās.

Ulūkāsyā (Owl-faced), Śvānāsyā (Dog-faced), Sūkarāsyā (Boar-faced), and Kākāsyā (Crow-faced), with their respective colors, arms, postures, and seats; those with the faces of donkeys, camels, cats, and goats, who are wrathful and devour entrails, sinews, and blood; and Yamadāḍhī, Yamadūtī, Yamadaṃṣṭrī, and Yamamathanī.

One should visualize [the deity] as Ardhanārīśvarī, with three faces, six arms, and three eyes; standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, naked, with loose hair, mounted upon a corpse on a universal lotus, and adorned with the five mudrās. She holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga, while another hand holds a severed head and a knife. She carries a *ḍamaru* drum and a vajra-spear, and is terrifying with bared fangs. She is adorned with a garland of fresh heads, wears a crown of skulls, is embellished by Vajrasattva and others, and her head is crowned by a crescent moon and a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*).

Just as with the Blessed One, so too for Vajravārāhī, the hand-gesture (mudrā) should be formed in the shape of the vajra-arm gesture; she is naked with disheveled hair and a girdle adorned with fragments, but her face is turned upward, being the white, terrifying face of a sow.

Just as it was spoken by Vajrasattva in the *Maṇḍalapaṭala* for the Yoginī according to the sequence of the *Pīṭhakrama* and the stated procedure for the *Lakṣāvidhāna*; and furthermore, it should be connected with the first and non-first chapters of the *Vajraḍāka-vidhāna*, the fifth which is the procedure for the *Ākṣepamaṇḍala*, and the *Mahāyogasamvara-vidhāna* consisting of the secret mystery (*guhyarahasya*) and the *ehi* [invocation]. Together with other heroic kings (*vīrarāja*) and ḍākinīs from all sides, there are various kinds of jars made of gold and silver, wrapped in variegated cloths and adorned with flower garlands.
Filled with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), endowed with the five medicinal herbs,
joined with the five jewels, and adorned with the five grains—
one should place sixteen [vases], or even two, in the cardinal directions and the intermediate points of the mandala.
To those who are intensely eager for various offerings to the ḍākinīs—
[offerings] consisting of naked beings with disheveled hair and various fierce substances—
one should surround the exterior of the maṇḍala with a garland of diverse corpses.
Outside of that, in the middle of the girdle, one sees the cremation ground, surrounded by Ḍākinīs, fashioned with various wonders, formidable and fierce;
and in front, the supreme maṇḍala, the assembly of gnosis.

Through the rituals of worship, the observances, the consecrations, and the successive stages, the wise one, having then become unified as one, should perform the deposition upon the body (*dehanyāsa*).
This includes the seats (*pīṭha*) of the heroes and yoginīs, the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, as well as the two types of armor (*kavaca*).
One should meditate upon all the wheels; having meditated, one should place the arrangement of body, speech, and mind within the heart of the Jñānasattva.
One should worship with various divine pledges (samayas) that are the most excellent of the Māras.
One should perform the recitation of knowledge (jñānajāpa) free from counting; it should manifest through the rosary of great numbers.
With a concentrated mind, one should perform the recitation using a rosary of great count.
Therein, the wise one should perform recitation with the worship and praise of the Samaya-maṇḍala;
through the application of benefiting and bringing welfare to sentient beings, and by the power of his aspiration,
the yogi will before long achieve the supreme reality of the Mahāyāna.
Oṃ śrīvajra he he ru ru kaḥ śrīḍākinījālasamvara hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ hrīḥ ha haḥ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ || [This is] the heart and the near-heart mantra.
Oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye hūṃ phaṭ || These are the heart and near-heart mantras of the goddesses.
Oṃ khaṇḍakapālina ka ka hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ mahākaṅkāla kuru kuru hūṃ hūṃ svāhā |
Oṃ caṇḍākṣī hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ kaṅkāla bandha 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ prabhāmatī hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā |
Oṃ, O you of terrifying aspect, terrify, terrify! Hūṃ 2 Phaṭ Svāhā!
Oṃ, O you with the great nose, Hūṃ 2 Phaṭ Svāhā! Oṃ, O enemy of the gods, agitate, agitate! Hūṃ 2 Phaṭ!

Oṃ drumacchāye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ aṅkurika phaṭ 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ airāvatī hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā |
Oṃ vajrajaṭila daha 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ mahāvajrabhairavī hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ mahāvīra paca 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā |
Oṃ vāyuvege hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ vajrahūṃkāra bhakṣa 2 vasarudhirāntamālāvalambine hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ surābhakṣi hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā |
Oṃ subhadra, seize, seize the snake dwelling in the seven netherworlds! Threaten, threaten! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Oṃ śyāmādevī hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Oṃ vajrabhadra, pull [it] forth, pull [it] forth! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!

Oṃ virūpākṣe jñoṃ 2 hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ khagānane hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ mahābala kṣmāṃ 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā |
Oṃ cakravege hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ ratnavajra hāṃ 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ khaṇḍarohe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā |

Oṃ padmanarteśvara sili 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.

Oṃ vajrasattva dhili 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ mahāvīrye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā ||
Oṃ ḍākinīye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ lāme hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ khaṇḍarohe hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā |
Oṃ rūpiṇī hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.

Oṃ sūkarāsye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.

Oṃ yamamathanī hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Thus, one should perform the visualization and recitation of the pledge-offering (*samayapūjā*) according to the sequence.
For the sake of welfare, one attains accomplishment (*siddhi*) and good fortune. It increases peace and nourishment;
it is the yoga that grants all desires, the most excellent of the excellent methods for piercing the egg (*aṇḍabheda*).
One succeeds according to the performance of one's karma; there is no doubt in this matter.
However, the unsurpassed perfection of yoga is obtained from the mouth of the Guru.
Alternatively, [one attains it] through the supreme sequence of all the seats of the Yoginīs.

Alternatively, she will speak of previously established matters in a dream. Through the great grace of the Yoginī, the unsurpassed state is attained. This secret, this mystery, this supreme commitment (*samaya*) is not to be disclosed.
The yogi [should practice] the supreme, most difficult yoga-yoga, which is the meaning of the secret essence.
In the Abhidhānottara, the eighth chapter is the "Chapter on the Attainment of the Pīṭhas."
